Medicare may be in trouble , but it be not go bankrupt .
 According to a 2021 report by the Biden administration , the Medicare Hospital Insurance ( HI ) trust fund will be deplete if healthcare expense continue to exceed money flow in .
 How the Medicare Trust Fund Works The Medicare HI trust fund support Medicare Part A .
 For people who be discharge from the hospital , it also cover short-term stay in skilled nursing facility or , a an alternative for people who choose not to go to a facility , it cover home healthcare service .
 Medicare Parts B , C , and D Only Medicare Part A be fund by the Medicare HI trust fund .
 Medicare payroll tax account for the majority of dollar that finance the Medicare HI trust fund .
 Taken together , these factor could deplete the Medicare HI trust fund at a rate not match the dollar come in .
 This decreased direct financing for the Medicare HI trust fund through payroll tax , at least for the short term .

Social Security and Medicare be still go bankrupt .
 At it current pace , Medicare will go bankrupt in 2026 ( the same a last year ’ s projection ) and the Social Security Trust Funds for old-aged benefit and disability benefit will become exhaust by 2034 .
 This annual report deliver yet another reminder to the American public that Medicare be undeniably go bankrupt .
 The report estimate that the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund will be bankrupt by 2026 .
 While the bankruptcy projection may snag the headline , there be three key budgetary number that shouldn ’ t go unnoticed .
 Reduction in Benefits in 2034 After the projected exhaustion of the Social Security Trust Funds , Social Security revenue will fund only 78 percent of promised benefit .

 These FAQs answer key question about Medicare financing and trust fund solvency .
 The different part of Medicare be fund in vary way .
 Funds for Part A benefit provide by Medicare Advantage plan be draw from the Medicare HI trust fund ( comprise an estimate 42 % of HI trust fund expense in 2021 ) .
 Funds for Parts B and D benefit be draw from the Supplementary Medical Insurance ( SMI ) trust fund .
 The solvency of the Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund , out of which Part A benefit be pay , be a common way of measure Medicare ’ s financial status , though because it only focus on the status of Part A , it do not present a complete picture of total program spending .
 This matter because when spend exceed income and the asset be fully deplete , Medicare will not have sufficient fund to pay hospital and other provider for all Part A benefit that be provide in a give year .
 For example , in 2021 , the Medicare actuary estimate that the HI trust fund would begin the year with $ 185 billion in asset , but because spending be estimate to exceed revenue by $ 15 billion this year , the trust fund be expect to end the year with $ 170 billion in asset ( Figure 2 ) .
 By 2025 , asset in the trust fund at the beginning of the year will have decrease to $ 73 billion , and with $ 50 billion more in spending than in revenue that year , asset will drop to $ 23 billion by the end of 2025 .
 In the 2020 Medicare Trustees report , the actuary project that asset in the Part A trust fund will be deplete in 2026 , just five year from now ( Figure 3 ) .
 A more recent projection from the Congressional Budget Office also estimate depletion of the HI trust fund in 2026 .
 While some describe the trust fund a head toward “ bankruptcy ” or “ go break ” , it be important to note that the Medicare program will not cease to operate if asset be fully deplete , because revenue will continue flow into the fund from payroll tax and other source .
 However , there be no automatic process in place or precedent to determine how to apportion the available fund or how to fill the shortfall .

There ’ s a remote chance Sanders could still win the Democratic nomination .
 But it would require an astonishing feat of political engineering .
 He will end the campaign close to even with Hillary Clinton in pledged delegate , and then make a persuasive argument to the party ’ s superdelegates , flip enough of them to his side to get him over the threshold .
 But a POLITICO analysis of the Democratic delegate math reveals that even under a best-case scenario , in which Sanders sweep the nine remain contest and pick up every undecided superdelegate still on the board , the Vermont senator would still need to persuade nearly 200 Hillary Clinton superdelegates to bolt from her camp — a feat of political engineering that would make the moon land look like a walk in the park .
 Sanders himself have say on multiple occasion that the more contest he win , the more pro-Clinton superdelegates would rethink their allegiance .
 In a late March interview on CNN , after win Democratic contest in Alaska , Hawaii and Washington state , Sanders say `` a lot of these superdelegates may rethink their position with Secretary Clinton .
 So they 're go to look at the strong candidate , and I can not see that any of them would look at Bernie Sanders a a strong candidate against a Trump .

, on Wednesday , say that the candidate with the most delegate from primary should be the party ’ s presidential nominee .
 Sanders , of Vermont , edge out moderate candidate who collectively win more vote .
 Dozens of interview with Democratic establishment leader this week show that they be not just worry about Mr .
 Sanders ’ s candidacy , but be also willing to risk intraparty damage to stop his nomination at the national convention in July if they get the chance .
 Sanders ’ s victory in Nevada ’ s caucus on Saturday , The Times have interview 93 party official — all of them superdelegates , who could have a say on the nominee at the convention — and find overwhelming opposition to hand the Vermont senator the nomination if he arrive with the most delegate but fell short of a majority .
 “ We ’ re way , way , way past the day where party leader can determine an outcome here , but I think there ’ s a vibrant conversation about whether there be anything that can be do , ” say Jim Himes , a Connecticut congressman and superdelegate , who believe the nominee should have a majority of delegate .
 Sanders , a democratic socialist with passionate but limited support so far , will lose to President Trump , and drag down moderate House and Senate candidate in swing state with his left-wing agenda of “ Medicare for all ” and free four-year public college .
 Historically , superdelegates have always support the candidate who win the most pledged delegate , which accrue from primary and caucus win .
 Sanders have demonstrate momentum in the race , win the most vote in each of the first three contest , he have yet to show that he can expand his coalition enough to set his campaign on a path to capture the majority of delegate .
 Sanders say that block him from the nomination if he have the most delegate would repel progressive , and would deliver a second term to Mr .
 Sanders on the top of the ticket could cost Democrats the political gain of the Trump era , a period when the party win control of the House , take governor ’ s mansion in deep red state and flip statehouse across the country .
 Sanders win big in the 16 state and territory hold primary and caucus on Super Tuesday next week , he could be on a path to the 1,991 pledge delegate need to capture the nomination on the first ballot at the party ’ s convention .

Ralph Morse/The LIFE Picture Collection via Getty Images In the complex dynamic of the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination contest , the most fascinating and confusing contingency involve a scenario where no candidate have a majority of the pledge delegate elect during the primary season .
 Now , pledge delegate aren ’ t legally bind to vote for the candidate to which they be pledge ( in the Democratic Party , at least ) , but most be select by campaign and be presumptively loyal .
 So the only way a plurality leader could win on the first ballot would be via the release of pledge delegate by a candidate who have withdraw from the race , or by convince just enough pledge delegate to defect on ground that a contested convention would damage and divide the party .
 That seem to be what Bernie Sanders be suggest at the recent Las Vegas candidate debate when he say the leader in pledged delegate should be grant the nomination even if she or he have no majority .
 Sanders probably have reason to believe that he would not benefit from proceed to a second ballot when 771 unpledged superdelegates ( mostly elect official and member of the Democratic National Committee ) — 16 percent of second-ballot vote — come into play .
 It would be an unsettling experience for everyone .
 Well , FiveThirtyEight now project that there ’ s a 50/50 chance that no candidate win a majority of pledge delegate .
